clue.text: Given name of Firbank enthusiast seems second-rate and inflexible

parts.note: B is the grade below A, so second-rate
inflexible means stiff, rigid

explanation.surface: A critic's devotion to Ronald Firbank is judged shoddy and narrow-minded.
explanation.walkthrough: The novelist and critic Brigid Brophy wrote a long study of the novelist Ronald Firbank; 'seems' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Brophy, the champion of Firbank's fiction, had the first name Brigid.

clue.text: I tire badly of Maestro Gaio

indicators.note: badly signals that the letters of the words I tire are put in a poor, scrambled order

explanation.surface: A singer complains of being worn out by the role of Maestro Gaio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' turns ITIRE into the composer's surname. The definition reads as 'the man of', that is the composer of, the opera Maestro Gaio.
explanation.definitionFit: Vittorio Rieti, the Italian-born composer, wrote the opera Maestro Gaio.

clue.text: Brothers with nobody to write about

definitions.text: Brothers with nobody to write about

parts.words: Brothers with nobody to write about
parts.note: two brothers who wrote a comic book about a Nobody, the clerk Charles Pooter

explanation.surface: Some siblings have no subject for their writing.
explanation.walkthrough: George and Weedon Grossmith wrote The Diary of a Nobody (1892); 'nobody' seems to mean no subject but points to the book's title.
explanation.definitionFit: The Grossmith brothers co-wrote the comic diary of the clerk Pooter, a self-styled Nobody.

clue.text: French writer is sort of dated around university

indicators.note: around means the reworked letters are placed round the next piece
sort of means a version of, so the letters of the word dated are rearranged

explanation.surface: A French author is judged old-fashioned on campus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' turns DATED into DADET; 'around' puts that round U, the university.
explanation.definitionFit: Alphonse Daudet was a nineteenth-century French novelist and story writer.

clue.text: He got the bird in Barnes

definitions.text: He got the bird in Barnes

parts.words: He got the bird in Barnes
parts.note: in a Julian Barnes novel a French novelist is linked to a stuffed parrot, the bird of the title

explanation.surface: A performer was booed off in Barnes, a district of London.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'get the bird' is to be jeered; Barnes looks like the London district but is Julian Barnes, author of Flaubert's Parrot (1984).
explanation.definitionFit: Barnes's novel follows a narrator hunting for the stuffed parrot the novelist kept on his desk.

clue.text: Calliope theme and variations from John Fuller?

definitions.text: Calliope theme and variations from John Fuller?

parts.words: Calliope theme and variations from John Fuller?
parts.note: a calliope is a steam organ, and the tune it plays gives the title of a John Fuller poetry collection

explanation.surface: A classical piece on the Muse Calliope, composed by someone called John Fuller.
explanation.walkthrough: Calliope looks like the Muse of epic poetry, but it is also the steam organ played at funfairs; John Fuller's first collection of poems (1961) bears the answer as its title.
explanation.definitionFit: A calliope pipes out the tunes heard at a funfair, and Fuller's book uses that phrase.

clue.text: Mrs Karenin has a schedule for the historian

parts.note: Tolstoy's Anna Karenina is the wife of Karenin
a schedule is a list

explanation.surface: Tolstoy's heroine keeps a timetable for a scholar of the past.
explanation.definitionFit: A chronicler who records events year by year is a historian.

clue.text: Powell's jewel of a countess

parts.note: a society beauty in Anthony Powell's novel sequence whose name is French for a jewel

explanation.surface: A novelist praises a countess as a gem.
explanation.walkthrough: Bijou Ardglass appears in Anthony Powell's A Dance to the Music of Time; her first name is the French word for a jewel.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for a gem names this glamorous character in Powell's sequence.

clue.text: Shares old elements in Hesse work

indicators.note: elements signals that the letters of the words shares old are taken as separate parts and rebuilt

explanation.surface: Stock market holdings are broken up in a German firm's dealings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'elements' breaks SHARESOLD into its letters to rebuild them; 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosshalde is a 1914 novel by Hermann Hesse about a painter's failing marriage.

clue.text: Location of Forester's marksman shows renewed good intention

explanation.surface: A sniper's island hideout stands for a fresh promise to do better.
explanation.walkthrough: Forester is the novelist C. S. Forester; his seaman Albert Brown holds off a German warship with a rifle from the island; 'shows' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: In C. S. Forester's Brown on Resolution a seaman snipes from an island so named; a fresh good intention is a New Year's pledge.

clue.text: Haggard's attachment to raptor

explanation.surface: A worn-out bird of prey has something fixed to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Rider Haggard wrote a novel called Jess; a short strap fastened to a falcon's leg has the same name.

clue.text: US poet offers drinks to Austrian composer

parts.note: gins are drinks
Alban Berg was an Austrian composer

explanation.surface: An American poet buys a round for a Viennese musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'offers' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Allen Ginsberg was the American Beat poet who wrote Howl.

clue.text: "Can a man be perfect if he never — or plays?" (E. M. Forster)

definitions.text: "Can a man be perfect if he never — or plays?" (E. M. Forster)

parts.words: "Can a man be perfect if he never — or plays?" (E. M. Forster)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap to fill: the missing verb is another sign of good humour, paired with playing

explanation.surface: Forster asks whether a man who never has fun can be perfect.
explanation.definitionFit: Forster's question pairs the missing word with playing, as two signs of merriment.

clue.text: Reportedly caustic author of beastly tales

indicators.note: reportedly means as spoken or heard, so the word for caustic is said aloud

parts.note: sarky is British slang for sarcastic, caustic

explanation.surface: A writer of animal stories is said to have a biting wit.
explanation.walkthrough: SARKY, British informal for sarcastic, said without its R sounds like the pen name of H. H. Munro, whose stories feature many animals.
explanation.definitionFit: Munro's stories such as Sredni Vashtar and Tobermory are full of savage or cunning animals.

clue.text: Joyce's heroic onehandled sinner

parts.note: in Ulysses Joyce describes Nelson on his Dublin pillar with this phrase, Nelson having lost an arm and had an affair

explanation.surface: A character in Joyce is a brave one-armed wrongdoer.
explanation.walkthrough: Ulysses calls Nelson, atop his pillar in Dublin, 'the onehandled adulterer'; Nelson lost his right arm and had an affair with Emma Hamilton.
explanation.definitionFit: Nelson's long affair with Lady Hamilton made him, in Joyce's phrase, a sinner against marriage.

clue.text: Germaine Greer's race

parts.note: Greer's 1979 study of women painters takes its title from a race over hurdles

explanation.surface: The feminist author Germaine Greer runs in a contest.
explanation.walkthrough: Greer's book The Obstacle Race (1979) is about the barriers faced by women artists.
explanation.definitionFit: Greer's title names a race over hurdles; the first word is a barrier in one's path.

clue.text: Grand Duchess in Anderson fairy tale?

definitions.text: Grand Duchess in Anderson fairy tale?

parts.words: Grand Duchess in Anderson fairy tale?
parts.note: Anna Anderson claimed to be a surviving daughter of the last Tsar, a claim later disproved

explanation.surface: A royal heroine appears in one of Hans Christian Andersen's stories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anderson fairy tale' suggests Hans Christian Andersen, but it is Anna Anderson's false claim to be the Tsar's youngest daughter; DNA tests later disproved it.
explanation.definitionFit: The youngest daughter of Nicholas II was a Grand Duchess whom Anderson impersonated.

clue.text: Foot of a peasant fractured

indicators.note: fractured means broken, so the letters of the words a peasant are broken and reassembled

explanation.surface: A farm worker has broken his foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fractured' rebuilds APEASANT; 'of' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A metrical foot of two short syllables then a long one, as in 'interrupt'.

clue.text: Tweedsmuir article describes Annan Water novelist

parts.note: John Buchan became Lord Tweedsmuir
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A Scottish peer writes a piece about a Border river.
explanation.walkthrough: Annan Water is a river in south-west Scotland and an 1883 novel by Robert Buchanan; 'describes' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish poet and novelist Robert Buchanan wrote Annan Water.

clue.text: English philosopher was in Spain yesterday

explanation.surface: A British thinker visited Spain the day before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'was' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A. J. Ayer wrote Language, Truth and Logic; in Spanish the same word means the day before today.

clue.text: Robert Adamson spread one in 1971

parts.note: the Australian poet Robert Adamson published a book with this title, and spreading one is passing on gossip

explanation.surface: A poet passed on some gossip in 1971.
explanation.walkthrough: One spreads gossip, and the Australian poet Robert Adamson published a book under that title in 1971.
explanation.definitionFit: Unverified talk passed from person to person is what one spreads, and Adamson's title names it.

clue.text: "Like a rich jewel in an —'s ear" (Romeo and Juliet)

definitions.text: "Like a rich jewel in an —'s ear" (Romeo and Juliet)

parts.words: "Like a rich jewel in an —'s ear" (Romeo and Juliet)
parts.note: Romeo says Juliet hangs on the cheek of night like a jewel in an African's ear; the gap takes Shakespeare's word for a Black African

explanation.surface: A line from Romeo's first sight of Juliet.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's word for an Ethiopian, or any Black African, fills Romeo's simile.

clue.text: Its towers apparently not yet complete in Marlowe's day?

definitions.text: Its towers apparently not yet complete in Marlowe's day?

parts.words: Its towers apparently not yet complete in Marlowe's day?
parts.note: Marlowe's Faustus speaks of the topless towers of Troy, and topless is read as having no tops built yet

explanation.surface: A city's towers were still unfinished in the playwright's time.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor Faustus asks, 'Was this the face that launched a thousand ships, / And burnt the topless towers of Ilium?'; 'topless', meaning too tall to see the top, is read as lacking tops.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the Latin name for Troy, whose towers Marlowe calls topless.

clue.text: Man's said to be magic in novel

definitions.text: Man's said to be magic in novel

parts.words: Man's said to be magic in novel
parts.note: Man sounds like Mann, and Thomas Mann's novel has a magic peak in its title

explanation.surface: A man is reputed to be a wizard in a work of fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Mann wrote The Magic Mountain (1924); 'Man's said to be' sounds like Mann's, so the novel is Mann's and the answer follows 'magic' in its title.
explanation.definitionFit: Mann's novel is set in a Swiss sanatorium high on a peak, the second word of its title.

clue.text: French composer seen in the Tiber, trying to get out

indicators.note: trying to get out pictures the letters of the river's name struggling and so jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A musician from France is spotted in Rome's river struggling to escape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trying to get out' scrambles TIBER; 'seen in the' is link material.
explanation.definitionFit: Jacques Ibert was a French composer, known for his Divertissement.

clue.text: Number of pieces preceding version of Rope by Brecht

definitions.text: Number of pieces preceding version of Rope by Brecht

parts.words: Number of pieces preceding version of Rope by Brecht
parts.note: Brecht's title is made of a German number, the German word for pennies, and a word for opera that rearranges rope

explanation.surface: Brecht's numbering of the scenes before his adaptation of the play Rope.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue spells out the title Die Dreigroschenoper (The Threepenny Opera): the answer is the number of 'groschen' (pieces) that comes before OPER, an anagram of ROPE.
explanation.definitionFit: German for three, the opening element of Brecht's Threepenny Opera title.

clue.text: Vaguely oriental setting of Goossens piece and Maugham play

definitions.text: Vaguely oriental setting of Goossens piece and Maugham play

parts.words: Vaguely oriental setting of Goossens piece and Maugham play
parts.note: a loose phrase for lands beyond the Egyptian canal, used as a title by both Eugene Goossens and Somerset Maugham

explanation.surface: Two works by Goossens and Maugham share a hazy Asian setting.
explanation.walkthrough: Eugene Goossens wrote incidental music for Maugham's 1922 play of this name, set in Peking.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase loosely means Asia, the lands beyond the canal linking the Mediterranean and Red Sea.

clue.text: Like C. E. Montague's values

parts.note: the critic C. E. Montague published a book of theatre criticism whose title pairs this adjective with values

explanation.surface: Someone shares the principles of the journalist C. E. Montague.
explanation.walkthrough: C. E. Montague of the Manchester Guardian published Dramatic Values (1911), a book of theatre criticism; 'values' looks like principles.
explanation.definitionFit: Montague's theatre reviews were collected under a title meaning values of the stage.

clue.text: Where Shylock was rated

parts.note: Shylock tells Antonio he has often berated him at the Venetian exchange

explanation.surface: Shylock was given a credit rating somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rated' looks like valued, but in The Merchant of Venice it means scolded: 'Signior Antonio, many a time and oft / In the Rialto you have rated me'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Venetian merchants' exchange, by the bridge, is where Antonio abused Shylock.
